# Kokālika Sutta (Snp 3.10 (PTS Snp 123))
**ID:** Snp 3.10 (PTS Snp 123)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Kokālikasutta* (Snp 3.10; also referred to as the *Kokāliya Sutta*) constitutes the tenth discourse of the *Mahāvagga* of the *Suttanipāta* [Silk 1994; Burlingame 1921]. In the narrative setting, the monk Kokālika, an associate of Devadatta, slanders the chief disciples Sāriputta and Moggallāna; despite repeated warnings, he persists, breaks out in severe boils, dies of the disease, and falls into hell [SuttaCentral; Marino 2017]. The Buddha then delivers an exposition describing Kokālika's rebirth in the Paduma hell and depicting the horrifying punishments awaiting those who speak evil or false words, such as being pierced with iron spears, traversing caustic rivers and forests of sword-leaves, consuming red-hot iron, and plunging into hell as a sheer precipice (*papāta*) [SuttaCentral; Marino 2017]. The discourse presents a distinctive cosmography of ten hells (beginning with Abbuda and ending with Paduma), measuring their immense durations via the simile of removing individual sesame seeds from a laden cart [Marino 2017].
According to the commentary *Paramatthajotikā*, the ancient *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* did not comment on the final two verses of the sutta, an omission indicating to commentators and modern scholars that these two stanzas were added to the text in Sri Lanka [Goonesekere 1967; Adikaram 1946; Kang 2012]. The commentary further notes that terms such as *abbuda niraya* do not denote distinct, individual hells (*paccekaniraya*), but specific periods of suffering endured in the Avīci hell [Silk 1994].
Close parallels containing matching prose and verse exist in the *Saṁyutta Nikāya* (SN 6.10, as well as SN 6.9) and the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* (AN 10.89) [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus; Marino 2017; Burlingame 1921]. Stanzas from the sutta also appear in the *Dhammapada* (Dhp 125, Dhp 306), *Udāna* (Ud 4.8), *Itivuttaka* (Iti 48), and the *Sāḷiyajātaka* (Ja 367) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus reveals extensive Pali reuse, notably in the *Brahma Saṁyutta* (SN 6), *Dasakanipāta* (AN 10), and the *Nettippakaraṇa* (Ne 37) [DharmaNexus; SuttaCentral]. Outside Pali, SuttaCentral and DharmaNexus record parallels across Chinese Āgamas (*Saṁyuktāgama* SA 1278 and SA2 276; *Ekottarāgama* EA 21.5) as well as verse collections including the Sanskrit Patna Dharmapada, the Gāndhārī Dharmapada, and Chinese and Tibetan recensions of the *Udānavarga* [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus further aligns passages of the text with Sanskrit and Tibetan treatises, including the *Āyuḥparyantasūtra*, *Karmaśataka*, and Nāgārjuna's *Suhṛllekha* [DharmaNexus].
